</start math nerding>
That's not what "negative volume" means. Dig a hole, the hole defines a certain volume. Fill the hole with plaster and make a mold. The mold has the same volume, but a presence where the hole was an absence. The mold is a "negative" of the hole, or vice versa if you prefer.

Volume is a vector quantity, like velocity; and a negative value just means the opposite direction from a particular frame of reference.

What this skip demonstrates is something else. Maybe a "non-adjacent contiguous volume". Meaning you can get to the affected location without passing through all the points normally between here and there. Which fits the part about getting his hand back.

The severing would be something else again. The earlier version mentioned in the comments where the hand was lost but still somehow connected fits better with the pure math. A discontinuity in the "graph" of his arm, but really still all part of the same "line".
</end math nerding>

An esoteric concept, but doesn't get caught up in the academic details and lose any non-technical readers. It deserves the nearly +200 it has at the moment.
Come on, folks, we're almost at 200! 10 more to go!!

item.content:encoded:
If it has zero mass and zero inertia, it's path would involve 0/0.

I'd expect it to be affected. If you take the limit as its mass approaches zero, it's affected. Also, General Relativity suggests that gravity is a fictitious force. It would be more accurate to say that an object in freefall isn't what's accelerating, the ground is.

It could just have a very tiny mass. If it's a membrane that somehow grew to immense area, it would have a mass comparable to an electron.

I wonder why it doesn't pass through solid objects. If it has no charge, it can't be the electromagnetic force, which is what normally keeps you from falling through the ground. My guess would be the electroweak force. I don't really know much about that though. The big question is why it has friction. I wouldn't expect that you could hold it with clamps.
